title: Snake bite
summary: Treat every snake bite as potentially serious. The aim is to slow venom spread, keep the person calm, and get to a hospital with antivenom as fast as possible.
steps: Move the person well away from the snake. Do not try to catch or kill it — a photo from a safe distance is enough.
Reassure the person and keep them as still as possible. Fear and movement speed up venom spread.
Lay them down on their side. Keep the bitten limb level with the heart and immobilised — splint as you would a fracture.
Remove rings, watches, bangles, and tight clothing near the bite before swelling starts.
Wash the bite gently with soap and clean water if available. Cover loosely with a clean dry cloth.
Note the time of the bite and where on the body it was. Mark the spreading edge of any swelling with a pen so doctors can see how fast it is moving.
Arrange the fastest possible transport to a hospital that can provide antivenom. Carry the person if you can — walking pumps venom around the body.
avoid: Do not cut, suck, or apply ice to the bite. Do not try to suck out the venom.
Do not apply a tight tourniquet — this can damage the limb and is no longer recommended for most bites.
Do not give the person alcohol, food, or aspirin/ibuprofen.
Do not waste time trying to identify the snake exactly — get the person to hospital.
Do not apply herbal pastes, cow dung, or other folk remedies to the wound.
whenToEscalate: Always emergency — every snake bite needs hospital review, even if it looks like a dry bite.
Especially urgent if: rapid swelling, difficulty breathing, drooping eyelids or facial weakness, bleeding from gums or wounds, dark urine, vomiting, drowsiness, or collapse.
Bites in children, pregnant people, or anyone elderly — extra urgent.
